   admission start and admission end times.

   a patient.

    or outcomes.

    conversation is synthetic.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with a complex history including systemic lupus erythematosus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, recent septic arthritis, and coronary artery disease presented with substernal chest pain concerning for acute cardiac ischemia. She was found to have elevated troponin and severe hyperkalemia, which resolved with dialysis and calcium. Due to a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, she was treated with bivalirudin and nitroglycerin for presumed unstable angina, though no acute coronary occlusion was confirmed. Her chest pain resolved, and cardiac medications were optimized, including increasing atorvastatin to 80 mg daily. She also underwent a left popliteal artery angioplasty for peripheral artery disease with gangrene of the left toes; amputation was planned as an outpatient. Her chronic gastrointestinal bleeding from gastric polyps persisted, precluding Plavix restart. She was discharged to an extended care facility with stable cardiac status, improved potassium, and ongoing management of anemia, vascular disease, and lupus.
problems: Atherosclerosis of native arteries of extremities with gangrene, left leg
Iron deficiency anemia secondary to blood loss (chronic)
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris

previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with a complex history including systemic lupus erythematosus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, recent septic arthritis, and coronary artery disease presented with substernal chest pain concerning for acute cardiac ischemia. She was found to have elevated troponin and severe hyperkalemia, which resolved with dialysis and calcium. Due to a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, she was treated with bivalirudin and nitroglycerin for presumed unstable angina, though no acute coronary occlusion was confirmed. Her chest pain resolved, and cardiac medications were optimized, including increasing atorvastatin to 80 mg daily. She also underwent a left popliteal artery angioplasty for peripheral artery disease with gangrene of the left toes; amputation was planned as an outpatient. Her chronic gastrointestinal bleeding from gastric polyps persisted, precluding Plavix restart. She was discharged to an extended care facility with stable cardiac status, improved potassium, and ongoing management of anemia, vascular disease, and lupus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in from dialysis with fever and shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a fever during dialysis and my heart was racing. I also felt short of breath when I walked, but that got better after a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chest pain, cough, or other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chest pain or cough. But I’ve had bad pain in my thighs for about three weeks. It’s burning and tender. My dermatologist thinks it might be calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. The skin changes on your inner thighs are concerning. We’ll consult dermatology. You also mentioned redness near your graft?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s sore and red on top of my left arm where the graft is. I didn’t finish dialysis because I felt so unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’re concerned about possible infection, so we’ve started antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—and gave you some fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be able to go back to dialysis soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll coordinate your next session. For now, we’re watching you closely. Your lactate was elevated, which can happen with infection or low oxygen to tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a sudden chest pain earlier, didn’t you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sharp pain on the left side, worse when I breathed in. It scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed some changes—ST depressions—which can indicate heart strain. We gave you aspirin, nitroglycerin, and pain medicine. The changes improved. Given your history of heart stents, we’re worried this could be a mild heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m on aspirin and my stents are old. Why now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes infections or anemia increase the heart’s demand. Your troponin is rising, which confirms heart muscle stress. We’re calling cardiology to help manage this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a CT scan to check for blood clots in your lungs. Good news—it ruled out pulmonary embolism. But we did see some bone changes related to your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the heart issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology agrees it’s likely a type 2 heart attack—caused by imbalance in oxygen supply and demand. Because of your GI bleeding history, we can’t take you to the cath lab right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they stopped Plavix because of bleeding. I’d rather avoid transfusions if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re using other medications to protect your heart. We started argatroban, a blood thinner that doesn’t use heparin, since you have HIT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your hemoglobin dropped overnight. And your stool tested positive for blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is the argatroban causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ve stopped the argatroban for now. You’ll have an endoscopy today to find and treat the bleeding site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team found a bleeding polyp in your stomach. They injected it with epinephrine to stop the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it bleed again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. They advised against repeat procedures unless it’s severe, since it could worsen bleeding. We’ll monitor your hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re confused tonight—talking a bit slower, drifting. We’re concerned about your mental status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel foggy. Is it the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. But your BUN is rising, and you missed dialysis. We think it’s uremia. We’ve scheduled urgent dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After dialysis, you’re more alert. That’s great. But your chest pain returned, and your troponin is still rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that same pressure. I used my nitroglycerin and it helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting argatroban because your heart issue is serious. But we’ll watch closely for any bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fast heart rhythm last night—ventricular tachycardia—but you were asleep and didn’t feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. We gave IV amiodarone, and it resolved. But your EKG shows a long QT, so we stopped amiodarone to avoid more arrhythmias.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more amiodarone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll rely on other heart medications and close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT because of your confusion. No stroke or bleed. It’s likely due to uremia and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics—are they helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are negative, but we restarted antibiotics because your lactate went up and you had low blood pressure. We switched to ceftazidime for dialysis dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now afebrile, and lactate is normal. We’ll stop antibiotics soon if you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my thigh pain? The pain meds make me confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dermatology recommends a fentanyl patch and tramadol. We’ll also start wound care with santyl and gauze. They advised stopping iron and vitamin D—they can worsen calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin peaked and is now coming down. That means the heart injury has stabilized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You still need rehab for strength and wound care. We’re sending you to an extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received intralesional sodium thiosulfate injections in your thighs today for calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurt, but I hope it helps. Why not the IV version?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your prolonged QT and VT episodes, we can’t risk IV sodium thiosulfate—it can affect heart rhythm. We’ll reassess if your QT improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid buildup in the lungs—likely from the fluids and blood transfusion. But no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit short of breath again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll adjust your fluids and monitor. Your heart function is okay, so this should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping antibiotics today. You’ve been infection-free for days, and cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue aspirin, atorvastatin, and a lower dose of metoprolol because of low blood pressure. We’re adding a fentanyl patch and oral dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped calcitriol, ferrous sulfate, and sevelamer. We started cinacalcet for bone health. Avoid calcium, iron, and vitamin D—they can worsen your skin ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 8.5. You received four units of blood during this stay, but no further drops since the EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Anemia and heart issues can do that. We’ll keep monitoring. You’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for a fistulogram as an outpatient to check your graft flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And dermatology follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call to schedule. Continue wound care daily. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to rehab. You’ve survived a tough hospitalization—heart attack, bleeding, infection, and skin issues—all managed carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been overwhelming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Keep using your nitroglycerin for chest pain, monitor your weight, and call if you have fever, black stools, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll follow up with your team.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and coronary artery disease presented with fever and shortness of breath from dialysis. She was found to have culture-negative sepsis, a type 2 NSTEMI with rising troponins and EKG changes, and an acute GI bleed from a gastric polyp requiring epinephrine injection. She developed transient confusion likely due to uremia, which resolved after dialysis. An episode of asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia occurred, managed with IV amiodarone, though it was discontinued due to QTc prolongation. Calciphylaxis in her thighs was treated with wound care and intralesional sodium thiosulfate, while IV therapy was avoided due to arrhythmia risk. Antibiotics were adjusted based on clinical course and dialysis needs. She stabilized, completed treatment, and was discharged to extended care with optimized medications, including fentanyl for pain, cinacalcet, and avoidance of QT-prolonging and calciphylaxis-exacerbating agents.
